passage: By Tuesday night Farida had seen the leopard clip five times: on the town news page, on two cricket-club accounts, on her cousin's status and on a page called Our Kasba Updates. Each caption said the same thing: "spotted near canal road, stay aleart." Farida lay on her charpai with the phone, heart jumping. The canal road was her road to school. Next morning she told Nandini, "Everyone's posting it. It must be true." Nandini took the phone and scrolled slowly. "Look. Same clip, same shaky tree, same time in the corner. Even the same spelling of 'aleart'." She tapped the oldest post. "They all copied this one." Farida read the caption again. It sounded just as true as before, which annoyed her. They walked the canal road together anyway, past the tea stall where the forest guard was laughing with the owner about "that old video".

qa.q: Where had Farida seen the leopard clip?
qa.a: On the town news page, two cricket-club accounts, her cousin's status and a page called Our Kasba Updates.

qa.q: Why was Farida annoyed after Nandini showed that the posts were copies?
qa.a: The caption still sounded just as true as before, even though she now knew all five came from one post, and that gap between knowing and feeling bothered her.

qa.q: What did Nandini do that Farida could use the next time a claim is everywhere?
qa.a: Scroll slowly, compare the posts and find the oldest one. If they share the same clip and spelling, it is one claim repeated, not five sightings.

qa.q: How might the forest guard see the rumour?
qa.a: The guard laughs about "that old video", which suggests it is a familiar recycled clip rather than a real sighting near the canal road.

grounding: A small-town teenager starts believing a leopard sighting because five accounts shared it, though all copied one post.

passage: Wei first saw it on Sunday: "City to ban phones in every high school from March!" By Wednesday it had turned up on a meme page, a gaming account, two classmates' stories and a video with dramatic music. Each time it felt a little more settled, like the weather. On Thursday at dinner in their Vancouver apartment, Wei announced it as fact. "Everyone's saying it." Xin, home from university for the weekend, asked, "Who said it first?" Wei shrugged. "Doesn't matter. It's everywhere." Xin scrolled for two minutes and turned the screen round. Every version linked back to one post from a joke news site, the kind that invents headlines for fun. The meme page had cropped off the joke label. Wei stared, then laughed a little too loudly. "I told my whole class," Wei said. "Now I have to untell them."

qa.q: Where did every version of the claim lead back to?
qa.a: One post from a joke news site, the kind that invents headlines for fun.

qa.q: How did Wei feel on seeing where the claim came from, and what shows it?
qa.a: Embarrassed 😅 Wei stared, laughed a little too loudly and remembered telling the whole class.

qa.q: Which question from Xin changed things, and how could Wei use it in future?
qa.a: "Who said it first?" Wei could trace a claim to its first post before sharing it, instead of trusting that it is everywhere.

qa.q: How might Wei's classmates feel when Wei has to "untell" them?
qa.a: Some may feel relieved and some a bit silly for believing it, and they may trust Wei more for correcting it honestly.

grounding: A teenager accepts a headline seen across many accounts until a sibling traces every copy back to one joke post.

passage: The hostel common room at the residential school outside Dehradun went quiet at nine, except for phones. Mohit, fifteen, had seen it six times since dinner: "Board order: hostel wifi shut from 9 pm for all Class 10 from Monday." A meme page, a quiz account, two seniors' stories, a video with sad music, a page that said NEWS in red. By the sixth, he stopped wondering and started downloading every chemistry video he might need. Sudha, from his class, looked over. "Scroll to the corner of each one." Mohit did. Every picture had the same tiny faded logo, from one joke page. The five others had just copied it. "Oh," he said. He'd been so sure. He kept downloading anyway, slower now, half laughing at himself.

qa.q: How many times had Mohit seen the wifi claim since dinner?
qa.a: He had seen it six times.

qa.q: Why did Mohit stop wondering after the sixth post?
qa.a: Seeing the same claim on so many accounts made it feel settled, as if six places meant six separate sources.

qa.q: What check could Mohit use the next time a claim shows up everywhere?
qa.a: He could look for where each post came from, like Sudha's tip about the logo, before accepting it.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel about pointing out the logo to Mohit?
qa.a: Sudha might feel a bit pleased to help, and hopeful that Mohit will stop panicking over a joke page.

grounding: A teen accepts a claim seen on six accounts, not noticing all copied one original post.

passage:
Dear Ramesh Bhaiya,
You'll laugh, but I need to tell someone who won't tell Mummy.
Okay, I did tell Mummy. That's the problem.
Last week I saw a post saying all schools in our district would get three extra weeks of summer holiday because of the heat. Then I saw it again on a cricket page. Then on my friend's status. Then on four more accounts. By the seventh time it felt like a notice from the principal. I told Mummy we could finally visit you in Nagpur, and she even started asking about train tickets.
Yesterday Sir laughed in class and showed us where it came from: one parody account. Everyone else had just copied it, word for word.
I feel so silly. Seven times felt like seven proofs. It was one joke, seven times.
Jatin

qa.q: Where did the holiday post really come from?
qa.a: It came from one parody account, and everyone else had copied it word for word.

qa.q: What does Jatin mean by "Seven times felt like seven proofs"?
qa.a: Jatin means seeing the claim on many accounts made it feel checked, even though it was really one source repeated.

qa.q: What turning point could help Jatin next time, and how?
qa.a: The moment Sir traced the post to one account; next time Jatin could look for the original before telling Mummy anything.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel after asking about train tickets?
qa.a: She may feel a little foolish or disappointed, though likely amused too, since Jatin believed it honestly.

grounding: A teen accepts a claim after seeing it on many accounts, not realising they all copied one post.

passage:
Hi Tenzin,
Remember I told you on Friday that the board is scrapping the practical exams this year? I was so sure. I'd seen it on at least six accounts: two meme pages, a coaching centre, some senior from another school, a "news" page, and my cousin's story. Six! It felt like everyone knew.
Today my physics sir asked where I'd read it. I opened the posts to show him and noticed they all had the same picture, same spelling mistake ("praticals"), and one tiny watermark in the corner. They were all copies of one post from a page I'd never heard of. Nothing on the board's website.
I felt so stupid. Six posts felt like six sources. It was really one.
Please don't forward what I told you.
Karthik

qa.a: All the posts spelled it "praticals".

qa.q: How did Karthik feel after seeing the watermark and matching mistakes?
qa.a: Karthik felt foolish and embarrassed, because six posts had seemed like strong proof but were really copies of one.

qa.q: What could Karthik check first the next time a claim shows up on many accounts?
qa.a: Karthik could look for the original post and check the official source, like the board's website, before believing or sharing it.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel reading this email?
qa.a: Tenzin might feel relieved to be warned and a bit grateful that Karthik was honest instead of letting the rumour spread further.

grounding: It shows a teenager accepting a claim seen on many accounts without noticing they all copied one original post.

passage:
So Minakshi asked me for this podcast what I believed online that turned out to be fake, and honestly, mine's embarrassing. I'm Nikita, I was fifteen.
There was this thing going round that the city zoo was shutting down and selling its animals to private owners. First I saw it on one reel. Then a friend reposted it. Then a page about animals. Then three more accounts in one evening. By the fourth one I wasn't even reading it properly. I just knew it. I cried a bit about the old elephant.
I made my mother call the zoo. The person there sounded tired. They'd had forty calls that day. Nothing was closing.
Later I went back and saw every single post had the same blurry photo of the gate. One post, copied everywhere, and my brain counted it as ten.

qa.q: What did the posts claim would happen to the zoo?
qa.a: That the city zoo was shutting down and selling its animals to private owners.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling by the fourth post?
qa.a: Nikita felt certain and upset, sure the claim was true and sad enough to cry about the old elephant.

qa.q: What small step helped here, and what could have helped earlier?
qa.a: Calling the zoo got the truth; noticing earlier that every post had the same blurry photo could have shown it was one post copied many times.

qa.q: What is it like for the person at the zoo getting forty calls in one day?
qa.a: They probably felt tired and worn down, answering the same false worry again and again.

grounding: It shows a teenager coming to accept a claim because it appeared on many accounts that were copying one post.

passage:
Monday. A reel popped up on Rafiq's phone: "From July, phones banned in all junior colleges in the state." He snorted and scrolled past.
Thursday. He saw it again, then again: a page for students, a cricket fan account, a classmate's story, a comedy page. At dinner he told his mother, "They're banning phones in college. It's all over." He felt the anger of it, the unfairness, as if it was already true.
Sunday. Vinita, his classmate, sent him four screenshots side by side. "Look at the font. And the little logo in the corner." The same meme page, copied by everyone. The education department had said nothing.
Rafiq stared at them for a long time. On Monday he'd laughed at it. By Thursday it had simply become something he knew.

qa.q: What did Vinita tell Rafiq to look at in the screenshots?
qa.a: The font and the little logo in the corner.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel about the ban by Thursday?
qa.a: He felt angry and treated it as unfair, as if the ban was already real, because he had seen it so many times.

qa.q: What went wrong between Monday and Thursday, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: Seeing the same claim again and again made it feel true, though it was copied from one meme page; next time Rafiq could check the education department before repeating it.

qa.q: How does Vinita seem to see Rafiq's belief?
qa.a: Vinita seems patient and clear-headed, showing him the evidence side by side rather than mocking him.

grounding: It shows a teenager coming to believe a claim over several days because many accounts copied the same meme post.

passage:
Nikita, you're sure because every page says it? Let your Vinita masi tell you about my Class 10 boards. Two days before the maths paper, one account posted, "MATHS PAPER LEAKED, EXAM WILL BE CANCELLED." By evening I'd seen it on twelve pages. Twelve! Different names, same words, same blurry photo.
I thought, if twelve pages say it, it must be true. I closed my books and watched films with my cousin. The next morning the exam happened. Nothing was cancelled. Later I found out all twelve had copied one boy's post, and he had made it up as a joke. I barely passed.
So tell me: how many of your pages copied the same one?

qa.q: What was young Vinita feeling after seeing the post on so many pages?
qa.a: She felt relieved and certain, sure the exam was cancelled because the claim seemed to come from everywhere.

qa.q: What turning point could have saved Vinita's exam?

passage:
In the middle of the May heatwave, the power had been out in Dolma's building for three hours, and her phone was on eight percent. She scrolled fast. "Schools closed all next week due to heat!" said one page. Then another. Then a page that looked like local news. Then her classmate Disha's story, with three fire emojis. By the time the phone died, Dolma had seen it six times and felt sure.
She didn't finish her science project; why rush if school was shut? Next morning the school bus honked at 7:15. Dolma ran out, project half-done, sweat already on her neck. On the bus, Disha admitted she had just reposted it from someone else, who had reposted it from someone else.

qa.q: What was Dolma's phone battery at?
qa.a: Eight percent.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when the phone died?
qa.a: She felt sure and relaxed, because seeing the claim six times made it feel solid.

qa.q: What could Dolma do next time she can't check an official source?
qa.a: Treat the claim as unconfirmed and keep preparing until the school itself says otherwise.

qa.q: How might Disha feel admitting she just reposted it?
qa.a: Disha may feel embarrassed and a bit guilty, since her repost helped convince Dolma.

grounding: Shows a teenager, unable to check properly, accepting a claim after seeing it on several accounts that were all copying one another.

passage:
In Jaipur, Ankita spent Sunday evening scrolling on the terrace. The same post kept appearing on different student pages: "Our school canteen uses week-old oil, share before they deleet!" Five accounts, then eight. By dinner she had told her mother, and by Monday she was refusing canteen samosas.
At lunch her friend Vinita asked, "Who actually found this out?" Ankita opened her phone to show her. Every post had the same spelling mistake, "deleet", and the same photo of a dark pan. She tapped back through the shares. They all led to one account, created two days earlier, with no other posts.
Ankita put the phone down. Somehow she still didn't feel like eating the samosa.

qa.q: What spelling mistake did every post have?
qa.a: "deleet"

qa.q: How did Ankita feel when she found the single source?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and a little foolish, yet the claim still felt true enough to put her off the samosa.

qa.q: What should Ankita do before telling her mother next time?
qa.a: Trace the shares back to the original and check whether it's one new account or real evidence.

qa.q: How might the canteen staff feel if the claim kept spreading?
qa.a: They might feel hurt and worried about losing customers over an unproven claim.

grounding: Shows a teenager accepting a claim seen across many student pages, then discovering they were all copies of one new account.

passage: I'm Santosh, and last month I nearly failed my biology project because of one claim. It said goldfish have a three-second memory. When I finally searched a real science site, it said goldfish can remember things for months. I had to rewrite a whole page at midnight. What still bothers me is how sure I felt, just because I'd seen it so many times.

passage:
School librarian's note, Class 9 research week

Nilesh came to the desk today with his essay on 'the Great Wall is visible from space'. He said he'd seen it on five different accounts, so it must be true. I asked him to open the posts again, one by one, on the library computer. His friend Raghav watched over his shoulder. The first two posts used identical wording. The third linked to the second. The last two were screenshots of the first. 'It's all one post,' Raghav said. Nilesh sat back and said, 'But it felt like everyone knew it.' I showed him how to find an original source, and we found a space agency page saying it is not visible to the naked eye. He is rewriting that paragraph. Next week I will run a short session for the class on tracing a claim back to its source.

Mrs Rao, librarian

qa.q: What claim was Nilesh's essay about?
qa.a: That the Great Wall is visible from space.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when he said 'But it felt like everyone knew it'?
qa.a: Nilesh felt surprised and a little confused, having trusted the claim because it seemed to come from many places.

qa.q: What will the librarian do next, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Run a class session on tracing a claim to its source, so students learn that many posts can be copies of one.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel after spotting that it was all one post?
qa.a: Raghav probably felt pleased and sharp, and maybe a little sorry for Nilesh.

grounding: A teenager sees the same claim across several accounts and accepts it, forgetting they were copying one original post.

13 Jan, night before Uttarayan.
The terrace is full of manja reels and Dadi's til laddoos are cooling in the steel dabba. Then this: a post saying police will fine anyone flying kites after 6 pm this year. First I scrolled past. Then I saw it on a kite-shop page, then on two meme accounts, then my cousin's story, then some news-looking page. Five places! By dinner I was telling Mummy we must wind up early tomorrow.
Yash called and asked, "Which account posted it first?" I said, "Everyone's posting it, so obviously it's real." He laughed and said all five had the same blurry police photo and the same spelling mistake, "fin". I didn't check. It just feels true now.
